# Glossary for Merlin

**Read in:** [UK English](uk/GLOSSARY.md)

The terms below occur in [*Merlin*](merlin.md), the English translation beside this page, and in the [Old French text](merlin-old-french.md) it was made from: Robert de Boron's *Merlin*, from the Huth manuscript (London, British Library, Additional MS 38117), as Gaston Paris and Jacob Ulrich edited it (Paris: Firmin Didot, 1886), volume 1, pages 1 to 146. The people and places come from Paris and Ulrich's name index and the old words from their word list, both in volume 2, cut to the entries these pages meet; the meanings are written in English from Paris and Ulrich's French glosses. A name is headed by the form a modern English reader knows, never by Malory's spelling, or by the 1886 edition's own form where there's no modern one, and every spelling the French uses is under *Also*, so a name underlines in both texts. Character notes say who somebody is when the story first meets them, not what later happens to them.

[^ryan-allen]: **Ryan Allen** designs and builds software. Good work disappears into what it's for. [ryanallen.com](https://ryanallen.com) · [GitHub](https://github.com/ryanallen) · [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ryanallencom) · [Leaftext](https://leaftext.com)

[^how-designed-the-system]: The tools that made this book, its checks and the rules they hold were designed as one system, and every line in it came out of that system. When a passage reads wrong, the fix goes into the system and the book is made again, never written in by hand, so it reaches every book on the shelf.

[^how-all-checks-passed]: Every range was run through the book's own check tool and the shelf's checks, and nothing was ticked done until they passed: a missing page, a broken link, an old word, a word repeated too soon, a wrong mark and a change nobody logged are all refused.

[^how-readable-first]: Each passage is told the way a good English writer would tell it today, then checked against the source so every event, person and act is there and nothing is invented.

[^how-plain-speech]: No Bible cadence and no stiff old-translation voice: no chains of "and… and… and", no solemn word order, no word nobody says now.

[^how-shaped-for-english]: Each sentence is written as English, not in the source's grammar: a verb rather than a noun made of one, never a clause hanging off a clause, and what someone must do before where or why, with nothing lost. Every sentence that says a common verb twice was read and either rewritten or kept with the reason.

[^how-every-link-said]: Where the source joins a cause and its effect with a bare "and", the English says how they connect, with "to", "by", "so", "until" or "because"; where it strings quotations together, the English says who speaks each one and why, never a bare "Again:".

[^how-nothing-said-twice]: What the source says twice, a doubled verb or a speech the narration has just told, is said once, unless a speaker repeats it on purpose, and the book's account of its text is given once, its edition and scans cited in full only under Sources.

[^how-the-right-word-each-time]: A source word with several senses takes the English its moment needs, never one word everywhere and never the vaguest.

[^how-no-word-worn-out]: No word comes back within forty words of itself, names and the commonest grammar words aside; the second use takes another word or goes.

[^how-modern-idiom]: Old English turns give way to the ones people use now, in how people talk to and about each other as much as in rare words: "pregnant", "said goodbye", "my mom". Every word judged old is kept in the shelf's list, and the check refuses each one.

[^how-us-english]: The reviewed US master uses Merriam-Webster spelling and usage, the article a US reader says, as "an herb", *The Chicago Manual of Style*, and lengths and distances in feet and miles. A later UK edition is made from that master.

[^how-natural-tenses]: The story is told in the simple past wherever the order of events is plain, as English tells it, not in the source's stacked past tenses.

[^how-neutral-tone]: No archaism and no color the source doesn't give, but a hard word stays hard.

[^how-gender-neutral]: Where the source means anyone, the English says "they", "people" or "anyone", never "he" and never a pair of pronouns; a figure the source names keeps the pronoun the source gives.

[^how-no-false-echoes]: No English turn that calls up a better-known story the source doesn't mean: Christ leads Adam and Eve out of hell, never "casts them out", which calls up Eden. An echo the source means stays.

[^how-read-aloud]: Every sentence or line was read aloud and its slack cut with no fact dropped; prose stays in paragraphs, and verse keeps its lines and stanzas, and its beat and rhyme wherever they survive.

[^how-scenes-read-for-movement]: Each whole scene was read for what each speaker wants and where it turns, and the whole book in order, so the dialogue and paragraph breaks carry it; nothing the source doesn't give was added.

[^how-sources-named]: Every reading says whose it is: the scholars who edited the text by name, the printing by its year, the handwritten copy by its own name, and this translation's own work as "this translation", never "we".

[^how-honest-where-unsure]: Where the dictionaries leave a passage open, it's translated as the scholars who edited the text read it, and the doubt is given in an endnote, never smoothed over.

[^how-fiction-called-fiction]: Each book's note opens by saying whether it's fiction or fact, and which parts were made up. A book is fact only when none of it was made up, so a history with any legend in it counts as fiction.

[^how-no-borrowed-wording]: Nothing was translated from Malory's English or any modern translation; they were used only to find where a passage sits in the legend.

[^how-source-over-malory]: Where Malory tells a passage differently, the source is the story and his version goes in a note; where sources are joined into one book, the one written first leads.

[^how-story-headings]: Every heading says what happens in its section, in a short plain sentence, so the headings alone tell the story, without giving away how a fight, a trial, a prophecy or a secret turns out.

[^how-laid-out-for-screens]: Laid out as a modern book read on a screen: a new speaker starts a new paragraph, no paragraph runs past 130 words, and the punctuation is a US book's.

[^how-malory-cross-referenced]: Where Malory's *Le Morte d'Arthur* tells the same passage, an endnote names his book and chapters; where it doesn't, nothing is said.

[^how-no-guessed-identities]: When a figure might be a better-known person from another book, the glossary says so only where the sources do; it never guesses.

[^how-no-common-words-glossed]: No ordinary English word is a glossary entry, since an entry is underlined on every page of every book that shares the glossary.

[^how-free-with-credit]: Anyone may use this book freely, crediting Ryan Allen, under the CC BY 4.0 license this book gives.

## New in this translation

An entry marked with an asterisk was written for this translation, not taken from Paris and Ulrich's lists of 1886.

## a bandon

Freely, holding nothing back: Uther's riders throw themselves between the Saxons' ships and their tents.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## abielir

To please.

## accomplissable

Also: acomplissables

One who carries something out.

## acorde

An agreement, a settlement.

## acoustumeement

As was the custom, regularly.

## acreanter

Also: acreanté

To promise, to guarantee.

## Adam and Eve

Also: Adan, Evain

The first man and woman in the Bible's Genesis. Yahweh made them and set them in the garden of Eden, but they ate the fruit it'd forbidden, and for that disobedience, Christians believed, every human soul afterward went down to hell at death. The story opens with Christ, after his crucifixion, going down into hell and freeing them and the other good souls, which is why the devils are so angry.

Wikipedia: [Adam and Eve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_and_Eve)

## adeser

To touch.

## adrechement

Guidance, direction.

## adrechier

Also: adrecha

To provide for, to settle in life.

## affaitier

Also: afaitier, affaitie

To mend or make ready; affaitie, well brought up.

## Agravain

Also: Agrevains

A son of King Lot of Orkney and Igraine's daughter, so Arthur's nephew, and one of Gawain's brothers. In the later romances he's the one who hates Lancelot and plots to expose his love for Guinevere, a part Malory keeps.

Wikipedia: [Agravain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agravain)

## aiole

A grandmother.

## ajorner

Also: ajornerent

To summon someone by letter to appear on a fixed day; the judges summon Merlin's mother to be put to death in forty days.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Alain

A kinsman of Joseph of Arimathea, son of Bron, who in Robert de Boron's story leads a company of his own westward as one of the Grail's keepers. Merlin tells Blaise that his story belongs in Blaise's book with Joseph's, joining the Grail's history to Arthur's.

Wikipedia: [Fisher King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher_King)

## alegier

Also: aliege

To grow lighter.

## Ambrosius Aurelianus

Also: Aurelius Ambroisius

The name Pendragon was baptized with, and the one the English called him by: in this story Pendragon is the older brother of Uther, son of King Constans, who comes back from exile overseas to take back his father's throne from the usurper Vortigern. The name comes from Gildas's real British leader of Roman family who rallied the Britons against the Saxons.

Wikipedia: [Ambrosius Aurelianus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambrosius_Aurelianus)

## amentevoir

Also: amenteues, ramentevés

To call to mind, to speak of.

## ams

Also: ambes

Both; d'ambes pars, on both sides.

## amuir

Also: amui

To lose one's speech.

## anemi

Also: anemis

The devil, and the devils as a host, said in the English as the devil: the French names them by it as often as by dyable, and the devil who fathers a child with the older sister is l'anemi.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Anglois

The French name for the English, which this story uses for the people Uther and Arthur rule. The romance calls Britain England throughout, never minding the difference between the Britons of Arthur's time and the English who came later and pushed them west.

## anvel

Also: anveus

Yearly.

## apenser

To make someone think.

## apert

Also: en apert

Open; en apert, openly, in front of everyone.

## ardoir

Also: ardera

To burn; burning is the death the law gives Merlin's mother if she can't name the child's father.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Arthur

Also: Artus, Artu

The son of Uther Pendragon and Igraine, whose conception Merlin arranges and whose childhood he hides, so that the boy grows up not knowing his own father. He's the hero the whole Arthurian legend gathers around, and this story tells how he came into the world and how the kingdom found him.

Wikipedia: [King Arthur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Arthur)

## assenement

Advice, guidance.

## asseoir

Also: assist le duc

To lay siege to.

## astronomie

Also: astrenomie

The art of reading the future in the stars; the seven clerks who know it read there that a child born with no earthly father will be their death.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## atargier

To delay.

## au Noel

Also: al Noel, dou Noel

At Christmas, one of the great feasts at which a king held court; Uther summons his barons and their wives to Carduel for it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## auctorité

Authority: the standing of a writing that may be cited as true, as the apostles' writings are; Merlin says Blaise's book won't have it, since Blaise isn't an apostle and writes what Merlin tells him, not what he's seen.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## aumosne

Charity, a good thing done for Yahweh's sake; Merlin tells Blaise that writing the book will be a great one.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## avoutire

Adultery.

## baceler

A young man not yet settled in life; the one the devil uses to seduce the first of the three daughters.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## baissiele

A maidservant.

## baptisier

Also: baptisiés

To baptize; the devils complain that the washing in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit takes men out of their power, and the holy man tells the mother to have her child baptized as soon as it's born.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## behourder

Also: behourde, behourdis, behourdé

To joust for sport with heavy lances that have no iron heads.

## Blaise

Also: Blaises

The holy man who hears the confession of Merlin's mother and stands by her. He writes down in a book everything Merlin tells him, so the story will be kept.

Wikipedia: [Merlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merlin)

## boine fin

Also: bonne fin

A good death: dying repentant and at peace with Yahweh, having given one's goods away for it. Merlin tells the dying Uther that a good death outweighs all the honors of a life, and that a bad one can lose all the good a life has done.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## boskillon

Also: boskillons

A woodcutter.

## Bretel

Also: Bretiaus

A knight of the Duke of Tintagel, Igraine's husband, who the duke trusts. In the story Merlin takes his likeness himself as part of the trick that brings Uther to Igraine, giving Ulfin the face of Jordain, the duke's other trusted knight, while Uther takes the duke's shape.

## Bron

Joseph of Arimathea's brother-in-law in Robert de Boron's Grail story, who catches the fish laid on Joseph's table beside the holy vessel, and so becomes the Rich Fisherman, keeper of the Grail after Joseph. Merlin tells Blaise that his story belongs with Joseph's in Blaise's book.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Fisher King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher_King)

## Candeler

Also: Chandeler

Candlemas, the Church's feast of the Presentation of Christ in the Temple on February 2. The barons ask for the sword to stay in the stone until then.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Carduel

A town of the Arthurian stories, which this one places in Wales, where Uther holds court. It's often identified with Carlisle, in northwest England, but the text doesn't tie it to a modern town.

Wikipedia: [List of locations associated with Arthurian legend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_locations_associated_with_Arthurian_legend)

## chainne

The Last Supper.

## chenu

White-haired; Merlin takes the shape of an old white-haired man to warn Uther.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## chouller

Also: choulloient

To play soule, a ball game played with crooked sticks.

## clarté

Light; the holy man tells the older sister always to sleep where there's light, because the devil hates light above all things.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## clergie

Learning, the knowledge of clerks, men schooled in letters; Vortigern's advisers say only clerks can learn by it why the tower falls.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## confanons

Banners carried on lances; the royal ones show the men on shore that the old king's sons have come.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## confessour

Also: confessours

A confessor, the one who hears a person's sins, sets their penance and advises them; the holy man who stands by the older sister is hers.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## congié de court

Leave to depart from a lord's court; the duke goes home without it, and Uther calls that a shame done to his court and summons him to answer for it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## consillier

To advise; also, to speak together in low voices.

## Constans

A king of England in this story, the father of three sons, Moine, Pendragon and Uther, and master of Vortigern, his steward. When he dies, the barons make his oldest son, Moine, king, though he's still a boy, and the story of Merlin's kings begins.

## contrait

Also: contrais

A cripple, a man who can't walk; Merlin sits by the road in that shape and begs of Uther.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## cotelle

Also: cotele

A short tunic.

## couvine

The way someone lives, what they do.

## creance

Also: creanche

Belief, faith; the Christian faith in which the holy man teaches the older sister.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## croche

The crooked stick soule is played with.

## cuingnie

An axe; Merlin comes as a woodcutter with one on his shoulder.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Damedieu

The lord god, from the Latin *Dominus Deus*, an old French name for the god used in oaths and prayers. This translation names it Yahweh.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## damoisiele

Also: damoisele, demoisiele

A young woman of good family, not yet married; the story's word for the older sister.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## dangier

Danger; the woman tells the younger sister that a woman given to all men is out of dangier, out of danger from the law that puts to death a woman taken in adultery.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## defensable

Able to hold out against an attack.

## dehait

Ill luck to, a curse on: Igraine answers Ulfin, who says she'll keep quiet, *Dehait qui s'en gardera!*, "a curse on whoever keeps quiet about it!"<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## dementer

To mourn aloud.

## desconneue

A mistake, taking one person for another.

## descouper

To clear of blame.

## desfier

Also: desfions

To defy: to declare openly that one owes a lord no more faith and will make war on him; the families of Moine's murderers defy Vortigern.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## despaner

Also: despanee

To tear; despanee, torn to rags.

## detraire

To tear apart.

## deus dragons

Also: doi dragon

The two dragons, one white and one red, that Merlin says lie under the water beneath Vortigern's tower. The older History of the Britons tells of a fatherless boy, a fortress that won't stand, and a red and a white serpent under a pool, and makes the red the Britons and the white the Saxons.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## devier

Also: devia

To die.

## devin

Also: devins

A soothsayer, one who tells what's hidden or the future; what people call Merlin.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Dieu tonant

god thundering: the noise of the battle at Salisbury is so great that nobody could have heard god thunder. It was an old French way of saying a noise drowned out everything, as people now say you couldn't hear yourself think.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## dist li contes

Also: dit li contes, se taist atant li contes

The story says: the storyteller's words for taking up a thread, *Chi endroit dist li contes*, "the story says here", set under a large initial, and *se taist atant li contes*, "here the story falls silent", for setting one down. The parts of this translation begin where the first stands.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## dormant

Sleeping; en son dormant, in one's sleep.

## doulouser

Also: dolousoit

To mourn, to be upset.

## dragon vermoil

The red dragon Merlin foretells, which flies through the air over the battle at Salisbury breathing fire, as the sign that the Britons will win; from it Uther takes the name Pendragon. Geoffrey of Monmouth tells instead of a star with a ray shaped like a dragon, and says Pendragon is "a dragon's head" in the British tongue.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Ector

Also: Auctor

A worthy knight of Uther's and Kay's father, who Merlin asks to take in a newborn child and raise him as his own son, his wife nursing the baby while Kay goes to another nurse. Ector agrees without knowing whose child it is. Malory's Sir Ector raises Arthur the same way.

Wikipedia: [Ector (Arthurian legend)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ector_(Arthurian_legend))

## edefis

Also: edefiemens

Buildings.

## Ekupedes

A kind of devil, in this story, that lives in the air, the kind that fathered Merlin. The word is found nowhere else; Paris and Ulrich guess it comes, garbled, from a word for centaurs, the half-horse creatures of Greek myth. The story makes them spirits, not gods.

## embarnir

Also: enbarni

To grow strong, properly to come to a man's strength.

## embatre

Also: embatirent

To drive in; s'embatre, to come across a place without warning.

## en conseil

In private, in secret.

## enchargier

Also: encarchier, encarka

To conceive a child.

## enche

Ink; Merlin sends Blaise for ink and parchment to write his book.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## encuser

Also: encuserai

To accuse.

## endementiers

Meanwhile; endementiers que, while.

## endroit de

Also: d'endroit

As for, as regards.

## engenreure

The fathering of a child.

## engien

A trick, a device of cunning: Merlin's word for the way he gave Uther the duke's shape.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## England

Also: Engleterre, Engletere

The southern and largest part of Great Britain, where most of this story takes place. The romance uses the name for the kingdom of Uther and Arthur long before there was any England, and doesn't draw its modern borders; it's simply the land the story's kings rule.

Wikipedia: [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England)

## englume

An anvil: the one of iron set on the block of stone, with the sword driven through it to the hilt.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## ensement

In the same way.

## ensiant

Knowledge; a son ensiant, as far as he knows.

## entechié

Also: entechie

Endowed with good qualities.

## entruesque

Also: entrues

While.

## erraument

At once.

## escommouvoir

To stir, to move.

## esmaiier

Also: esmaiiés

To dismay; to lose heart.

## esperir

To wake up.

## estavoir

Also: estavoirs

What one needs, necessities.

## estore

A fleet.

## fisike

Medicine, the learned art of healing and of the nature of things; for her knowledge of it Morgue is called Morgan le Fay.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## forche d'art

By force of art: Merlin's skill, by which he brings over from Ireland the stones the king's men couldn't move.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## gabés

Also: se gabe

To mock, to make fun of: Ulfin tells Igraine she may be mocking him.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Gaheris

A son of King Lot of Orkney and Arthur's half-sister, and so Gawain's brother. Here he's named only among Lot's children; in later romances, and in Malory, he grows up to be one of the knights of Arthur's court.

Wikipedia: [Gaheris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaheris)

## galilee

A porch or chapel at the entrance to a church; the block of stone appears before the church door, in front of it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## garandir

Also: garandi, warandir

To protect, to keep from harm or death.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## garce

A girl, a woman of low birth; Kay was nursed on the milk of one so that Arthur could have his mother's. It carries none of the insult of the modern French word.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## garchon

Also: garchons

A low fellow, a thug; the younger sister brings a crowd of them to her sister's house, and they beat her.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Gareth

A son of King Lot of Orkney and Arthur's half-sister, and so Gawain's brother. Here he's named only among Lot's children; in Malory he becomes the hero of his own tale, the kitchen boy called Beaumains who proves himself a knight.

Wikipedia: [Gareth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gareth)

## garsoil

A word that a passage Paris and Ulrich added says Hengist's daughter was the first to say in England. Geoffrey of Monmouth tells of a daughter of Hengist who greets Vortigern at a feast with a cup of wine and an Old English wish of health, and dates from it the drinking greeting of Britain.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## gastine

A waste, a wilderness: the *deserte gastine* where Joseph's people go hungry after Christ's death.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Gawain

Also: Gauvain, Gauvains

A son of King Lot of Orkney and Arthur's half-sister, named here among Lot's children. In later romances, and in Malory, he becomes one of the greatest of Arthur's knights, his nephew and his champion.

Wikipedia: [Gawain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gawain)

## genvre

Young; a child.

## guenchir

Also: guenchi

To turn aside, to wheel about.

## harnas

Baggage and gear: the duke's knights leave theirs behind and keep only their arms and horses, to ride away by night unseen.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Hengist

Also: Hangus, Hanguis, Hangu

The leader of the Saxons, the pagan people from across the North Sea who come into Britain in Vortigern's time. Vortigern takes him and his men into his service to fight for him, and Hengist's Saxons become the Britons' great enemy.

Wikipedia: [Hengist and Horsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hengist_and_Horsa)

## herbegier

To take lodging for the night.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## heudure

The guard of a sword, the crosspiece between blade and grip; Arthur takes the sword from the stone by it.

## heut

The hilt of a sword.

## hoir

An heir; Merlin tells Uther he's gained one and must give it up to Merlin, and at Uther's death the land is left without one.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Holy Grail

Also: saint graal, graal

The holy vessel of Joseph of Arimathea's story, the cup Christ used at the Last Supper, in which Joseph caught his blood at the cross, as Robert de Boron told in his *Joseph*. Merlin tells Blaise he'll go to live among the people who keep it, and that Blaise's book will join theirs.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Holy Grail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Grail)

## homme sauvage

A wild man, one who lives in the woods apart from other people; Merlin comes as a woodcutter so shaggy and long-bearded that he looks like one.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## hosel

Also: housiaus

A legging that covers the leg from ankle to knee.

## houmages

Homage, the vow by which a vassal became a lord's man and held land from him; Arthur will take none until he's crowned.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## hounours

Honors: worldly rank, and the lands and offices that go with it, which a vassal holds from a lord; the barons ask Arthur to give them back theirs to hold from him.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## hurepé

Also: hurepés

With hair in disorder, shaggy.

## Igraine

Also: Ygerne, Igerne

The wife of the Duke of Tintagel, famous for her beauty and her goodness, who catches King Uther's eye when the barons come to his court with their wives. She's faithful to her husband and wants nothing to do with the king's attentions.

Wikipedia: [Igraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igraine)

## Ireland

Also: Irlande

The large island west of Great Britain, across the Irish Sea, which Rome never ruled. Its people raided and settled the west of Britain in the centuries after the Romans left, and its monks carried Christianity back to Britain and beyond.

Wikipedia: [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland)

## iretage

An inheritance, the lands and wealth a person holds from their family; the older sister's from her dead father.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## jehir

To confess, to own up.

## Jesus Christ

Also: Jesucrist, Jesucris, Jhesucrist, Jesus

The son of Yahweh in Christian belief, who Christians hold died on the cross and rose again. The story opens on the belief that after his death he went down into hell and freed the good souls the devils held there, Adam and Eve among them, which is why the devils plot their revenge.

Wikipedia: [Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus)

## Jordain

Also: Jourdain, Jourdains

A knight of the Duke of Tintagel's household, one of the men closest to him, with Bretel. He's one of the few at Tintagel the story names, and Malory leaves him out.

## jornee

Also: jornees

A day's journey; to go by one's jornees is to travel by day's stages.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Joseph of Arimathea

Also: Joseph

A rich follower of Jesus who, the Gospels say, asked Pilate for Christ's body and laid it in his own tomb. Robert de Boron's *Joseph* made him the first keeper of the Holy Grail, the cup in which he caught Christ's blood, and Merlin has Blaise write Joseph's story into the same book as his own.

Wikipedia: [Joseph of Arimathea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_of_Arimathea)

## jovle

Young.

## Judas

The apostle who betrayed Christ to his enemies for thirty pieces of silver and then hanged himself. Merlin tells Uther that Joseph of Arimathea's table had an empty seat for the place Judas left at the Last Supper, and that Uther's table will have one too.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Judas Iscariot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judas_Iscariot)

## jungnet

July, "little June": Merlin tells the brothers the Saxons will land on its eleventh day.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## justiche

Justice in its hard sense, punishment by law; to do justiche of someone is to put them to death.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Kay

Also: Ké, Kés

Ector's own son, nursed by another woman so his mother can nurse the baby Merlin brought, and brought up as that child's brother. In Malory and the later romances he becomes Arthur's seneschal, the steward of his household, known for his sharp tongue.

Wikipedia: [Sir Kay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Kay)

## King Lot

Also: Loth

King of Orkney, who marries one of Igraine's daughters by the Duke of Tintagel. Orkney is the group of islands off the north of Scotland. The marriage is part of the peace made with the duke's family, and their children are Mordred, Gawain, Agravain, Gareth and Gaheris, as the story names them.

Wikipedia: [King Lot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Lot)

## laidengier

To insult, to abuse.

## liges

Liege, bound to a lord before all others; Uther calls the respected man who'll raise the child his liege man.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## lignage

Also: lingnage

A person's relatives, their whole family; the relatives of Moine's murderers take up the wrong done to them and make war on Vortigern.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## litiere

A stretcher, a bed on two poles carried by men or slung between two horses; Merlin tells the sick Uther to have himself carried on one to the battle.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## liue

A measure of road, about three miles; the peasant goes no more than half of one, a mile and a half, before he falls dead.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## livre des prophecies

The Book of the Prophecies of Merlin, begun when the king and his people resolve to write down whatever Merlin foretells; it holds only what he says, not who he is or where he came from. Geoffrey of Monmouth put a *Prophecies of Merlin* into his history of the kings of Britain.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Logres

The Britons' legendary kingdom, which Uther rules, and in this story also its chief city, where he holds court and dies. Neither is on a modern map.

Wikipedia: [Logres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logres)

## loiier

A reward, a fee paid for a service; the old man asks what reward the king will give.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## London

Also: Londres

The city on the Thames in southeastern England, already the greatest town of Britain under the Romans. Here, after the battle of Salisbury, Uther is crowned king, and the barons gather there for the great feasts of the year.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London)

## los

Advice.

## maistre eglise

The chief church of the city, where Arthur keeps his vigil and is crowned.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## mar

What a pity; to one's cost.

## martyre

Also: day of her execution

Martyrdom: a death suffered for one's faith, as the saints suffered theirs; the women and the judges give the name to the burning Merlin's mother is sentenced to, a death she's to suffer innocent, and the English says it as her execution.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Mary

Also: sainte Marie

The mother of Jesus Christ, who Christians believe conceived him as a virgin by the Holy Spirit. She was the most honored of all saints in the Middle Ages, prayed to for help in every need, which is why the older sister calls on her when she wakes in terror.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Mary, mother of Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary,_mother_of_Jesus)

## menistres

Also: menistre

The clergy, who the devils say Christ left on earth to save sinners who repent and do as the clergy tell them.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Merlin

Also: Merlins, Mierlin, Mierlins

The child the devils plot to father on a devout young woman, to undo what Christ won. From his father he has the knowledge of everything that's been done and said; Yahweh, for his mother's goodness and her repentance, gives him knowledge of the future too, and leaves him free to choose which side to serve.

Wikipedia: [Merlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merlin)

## mesaesmer

Also: mesaesmeroit

To look down on, to despise.

## mescheoir

Also: meskeu

To go badly for someone.

## meserrer

Also: meserra

To lose your way, or go wrong.

## Moine

King Constans's oldest son, who'd been made a monk, and who the barons make king after their father dies, though he's still young. Vortigern, the old king's steward, runs the kingdom for him.

## monter

Also: monte

To matter, to amount to; also, to climb.

## Mordred

Also: Mordrès

A son born to King Lot's wife, named first among Gawain's brothers. In the oldest record, the Welsh annals, a Mordred falls with Arthur at Camlann; later romances, and Malory, make him Arthur's betrayer.

Wikipedia: [Mordred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mordred)

## Morgan le Fay

Also: Morgue

A daughter of Igraine's. Uther sends her to a house of religion to learn to read and write, and there she learns the seven arts, astronomy and medicine.

Wikipedia: [Morgan le Fay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_le_Fay)

## Morgans

A daughter born outside marriage, the one King Nentres of Sorhaut marries. Paris and Ulrich's name index runs her and Morgue together, but the French text names them apart.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## mostres

A portent, a sign shown in the sky: the red dragon is the one Merlin promised.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## moustier

A church; Pendragon is coming back from one when the next stranger comes to him.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Nentres

King of Sorhaut, who marries Morgans, another of Igraine's daughters, born outside her marriage. Malory calls him King Nentres of Garlot, married to Igraine's daughter Elaine, and has him fight against the young Arthur.

Wikipedia: [King Nentres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Nentres)

## nonains

Nuns; Merlin takes the messengers to the house of nuns where he's had his mother take the veil.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## norriche

A nurse who suckles another woman's child. Ector blames Kay's faults on the nurse whose milk he drank in Arthur's place, since a child was thought to take its nature from the milk it sucked.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Northumberland

Also: Norhomberlande

The far north of Britain, where Merlin sends Blaise to write his book, a wild country thick with great forests. The name means the land north of the Humber; the romance gives it no modern borders.

Wikipedia: [Northumberland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumberland)

## nueches

A wedding; Uther and Igraine's is held on the thirteenth day after the two weeks that followed the peace talks.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## ochoison

A cause, a reason.

## oes

Use, behalf; a son oes, for himself.

## oirre

A road, a journey.

## Orkney

Also: Orkenie, Orkanie

The islands off the north tip of mainland Scotland, which the romances make King Lot's kingdom, so that Lot of Orkney, husband of Arthur's half-sister, is one of the great kings of the story. In history the islands were home to the Picts, then taken by Norse settlers from the ninth century CE.

Wikipedia: [Orkney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orkney)

## ostoiier

To make war.

## palefrois

Riding horses, rather than horses for war; the Saxons offer a hundred a year as tribute with knights, young women, falcons and greyhounds, and the baron who tests Merlin rides one.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## pavillon

Also: paveillon

A large tent, a king's or a lord's lodging in camp; Hengist comes alone by night to Uther's to kill him.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## pelerinage

A pilgrimage, a journey to a holy place; the peasant has bought leather to mend his shoes for one.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Pendragon

Also: Pandragon, Pandragons

King Constans's second son, Uther's older brother, still a boy when their father dies. His name holds the word *dragon*, as the story will explain.

Wikipedia: [Pendragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pendragon)

## penitanche

Also: penitance

Penance, what a confessor sets a sinner who has confessed to make amends; the holy man sets the older sister one for all her life.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Penthecouste

Pentecost, the Church's feast of the Holy Spirit's coming to the apostles, one of the great feasts at which a king held court. The brothers hold court at it by the river as the Saxons come, and Uther founds his table at it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## perron

A great block of stone, four-sided and thought to be marble, that appears before the church on Christmas morning with an anvil on it and a sword through the anvil.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## pierres d'Irlande

Also: chimentiere de Salesbieres

The great stones Merlin has brought from Ireland by his art and sets upright over the dead of Salisbury in the burial ground, where the story says they still stand. Geoffrey of Monmouth calls them the Dance of the Giants and has them fetched from Mount Killaraus in Ireland, and says the ring of stones near Salisbury is called Stonehenge in English.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## plege

Also: plegerons, plegié

Someone who vouches for another's promise with their own life or goods; the messengers vouch for Merlin with their lives, and he calls them the men who vouched for him.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## pourcach

Contriving, scheming.

## pourcachier

Also: pourcacha, porcache, porchacié, pourcache, pourcachiés, pourcachoit, porcachier, pourcacier

To work at, to contrive; to get for someone.

## prendre samblance

Also: pris samblanche, pris le samblance, prist la samblance

To take on a shape or a likeness not one's own, as the devils say one of them can take a man's.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## preudefeme

Also: preudefemes

A decent woman, upright and respected; the French says it of Igraine as it says *preudom* of a holy or respected man.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## prevoire

Also: prouvoire, prestre

A priest; the judge's mother's priest, who Merlin says is the judge's true father.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## privés

Those closest to a lord, the people he trusts with his secrets; Uther tells two of his how he longs for Igraine.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## prophete

The prophets of the Old Testament, who predicted that the son of Yahweh would come to earth; the devils say they took them for it and held them in hell.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## puciele

Also: pucieles

A girl not yet married.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## quinsainne

Two weeks; the day fifteen days off that Merlin and the judge set for the judge's mother to come.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## raplegier

To vouch for someone with your own life or goods.

## regnavle

Also: regnaule

Fitting, right.

## reponre

Also: reposte

To hide.

## reveler

Also: revelerent

To rebel.

## Rome

Also: Romme

The city in central Italy where the pope, the bishop of Rome, has his seat, the center of the Western Church. The story's "law of Rome" means the Christian faith as the Church at Rome taught it, which converts were baptized into.

Wikipedia: [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome)

## Round Table

Also: table reonde, tierche table

The third table, which Merlin bids Uther found in the name of the Trinity after the table of the Last Supper and Joseph's table. He makes it at Carduel and seats fifty of the worthiest men of the land at it, with one place left empty.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Round Table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round_Table)

## sacre

The crowning of a king and his anointing by the archbishop; until it's done, Arthur won't call himself lord of the kingdom.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## saint esperit

Also: Holy Spirit

The Holy Spirit; the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are named together in the washing of baptism and in the sign of the cross.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## saint Martin

Saint Martin's Day, the feast of Saint Martin of Tours on November 11; Uther dies in the two weeks after it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Salisbury

Also: Salesbieres

The plain around Salisbury, in Wiltshire in southern England, a wide open upland of chalk. This story sets the Britons' great battle with the Saxons there, where the two brothers lead their army against Hengist's host.

Wikipedia: [Salisbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salisbury)

## Satan

Also: Sathanas

The devil by name, the fallen angel Christians hold rules over hell and tempts people to sin. The story opens on his fury that Christ freed the souls hell held, and the judge's mother swears by him.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Satan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satan)

## saudees

Wages, pay; Merlin speaks of the glorious reward Joseph had for the body of Christ.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## sauve s'ounour

So long as it's honorable: the one limit set on the gift Uther swears to give Merlin before he knows what it is.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Saxons

Also: Saisnes, Saisne, Saxon

The heathen people from over the sea who come to win England in this story, against who Uther and Arthur fight. The real Saxons were one of the Germanic peoples from the North Sea coast, today's northern Germany and Denmark, who settled Britain in the fifth and sixth centuries and became the English.

Wikipedia: [Saxons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxons)

## segnier

Also: sainne, sainna, sainnierent, saingnierent

To make the sign of the cross on oneself; the holy man tells the older sister to do it every time she lies down and gets up, so that the devil can't trick her.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## semonre

To summon one's people to arms; Vortigern summons his to meet the brothers' landing.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## senefiance

Also: senefiances, senefianche, senehances

A meaning, what a sign stands for; Merlin says the dragons' fight has a great one.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## senescal

Also: senescaus

A steward, the officer who ran a king's household and lands for him, the greatest officer of the court; Vortigern is King Constans's and then King Moine's.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## seri

Also: serie

Calm, still.

## serjans

Also: serjant

A servant who does someone's errands; the older sister sends hers for two women, and the herder in the forest calls himself one.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## set ars

The seven liberal arts, the course of learning of the medieval schools: grammar, rhetoric and logic, then arithmetic, music, geometry and astronomy. Morgue learns all seven.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## sollers

Also: saullers

Shoes.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## sor sains

On relics, the remains of saints; Vortigern makes his messengers swear on them that they'll kill the fatherless child.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Sorhaut

King Nentres's kingdom in this story. Later French romances make Sorhaut a city, the chief town of King Urien's land of Gorre, and Malory gives Nentres the land of Garlot instead; no source places it on a modern map.

## sortir

Also: sorti, sortirent

To foretell by divination; in this story, the clerks reading the stars, the art the text calls astronomy.

## sourconsillier

Also: sourconsilla

To give bad advice.

## Te Deum laudamus

Latin, "We praise you, Yahweh," an old Latin hymn of thanks still sung in churches at moments of great joy, as at a coronation or a victory. The clergy sing it when the sword in the stone is found.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Te Deum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Te_Deum)

## teche

Also: teches

A quality, a trait.

## Tintagel

Also: Teintaguel, Tintaguel, Tintageul

The coastal headland in Cornwall where this story places the castle of the duke whose wife is Igraine. The castle visible there today was built centuries later.

Wikipedia: [Tintagel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tintagel)

## toises

A measure of length, about six and a half feet; Vortigern's tower stands three or four of them, twenty feet or so, above the ground before it falls each time.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Toussains

All Saints' Day, November 1, the Church's feast honoring every saint, known and unknown, and one of the great feasts when a king held court. Ector makes his son Kay a knight on it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## trinité

Also: trinités

The Trinity, the god as Father, Son and Holy Spirit; the heathen Saxons don't believe in it, and Merlin bids Uther found the third table in its name.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## trives

A truce: the king's men ask the Saxons in their castle for one of three months.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Ulfin

Also: Urfin, Urfins

An adviser of Uther's, the one the king trusts with his secret love for Igraine, who carries his messages and gifts to her. Malory calls him Sir Ulfius, one of Uther's knights.

Wikipedia: [Gorlois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorlois)

## Ursin

Also: Ursins

An adviser of Pendragon's, sent with two others to ask the Saxons for a truce. He's one of the few of Pendragon's men the story names, and he's known only from this passage.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Uther

Also: Uther Pendragon, Uter, Uters, Uter Pandragon, Uters Pandragons

King Constans's youngest son, Pendragon's brother, still a boy when their father dies. In British legend he's Uther Pendragon, the best known of the story's kings.

Wikipedia: [Uther Pendragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uther_Pendragon)

## vaissiel

A vessel; the holy vessel of Joseph's story, the word Merlin uses for his mother, the vessel the devils put him in, and a ship, as the ships Pendragon and Uther bring home.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## vallet

Also: vallès, varlès

A young man; also a young servant, as the older sister's is.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## veilla

Kept vigil: the night after the archbishop makes him a knight, Arthur stays awake in prayer in the chief church until day.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## viers orient

Toward the east, where Pendragon's and Uther's guardians take them, because their ancestors came from there. Geoffrey of Monmouth's History of the Kings of Britain, an older telling, sends them over the sea to Brittany.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## viespres

Also: viespre

Evening, the hour of vespers; Pendragon waits for Merlin until it's past.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## vieut

Empty.

## vilain

Also: vilains

A peasant, a man of low birth who works the land.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Vortigern

Also: Vertigier, Vertigiers

King Constans's steward, the most powerful man at court, who runs the young King Moine's affairs for him. In British legend he's the king who invited the Saxons into Britain.

Wikipedia: [Vortigern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vortigern)

## Wales

Also: Gales

The country on the western side of Great Britain, where the Britons held out after the Saxons took the east. This story places Carduel, one of Uther's and Arthur's chief cities, there, though later romances put Carduel at Carlisle in the north of England.

Wikipedia: [Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales)

## Winchester

Also: Wincestre

A city in Hampshire, inland in southern England, the old capital of Wessex. This story makes it a seaport, where Pendragon and Uther land with their army when they come back to take their kingdom.

Wikipedia: [Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winchester)

## Yahweh

The name of the god of the Israelites in the Hebrew Bible, the one god Jews and Christians worship, written in Hebrew with four letters, YHWH. Jews stopped saying the name aloud before Jesus's time and said "my lord" instead, so the Greek and Latin Bibles wrote "lord" where the name stood, and the Latin and French of these books call it only god or lord, never by its name. This translation gives the god its name wherever the source speaks of it, and calls it "it", as it would any people's god.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Yahweh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahweh)
